source.title: Signal Propagation in Transformers: Theoretical Perspectives and the Role of Rank Collapse
source.authors: Lorenzo Noci; Sotiris Anagnostidis; Luca Biggio; Antonio Orvieto; Sidak Pal Singh; Aurélien Lucchi

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Analyzes and empirically evaluates how initialization, residual scaling, depth, and normalization affect signal propagation and training in Transformers, bearing on V3 and V4 through different measures and architecture.
record.gate_note: Reports results about token correlation, gradient norms, and IWSLT14 translation training. The paper does not test CIFAR classification error, two-layer teacher-student local minima, above-stability learning rates, or batch normalization's accuracy-speed effect. Results cited from prior work are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The study reports original Transformer results, but none tests the specified versions. Token correlations and initialization gradient norms do not measure training speed or trainable depth in plain networks; translation BLEU does not establish the specified convolutional training-error effects. Layer normalization is not batch normalization.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors link identical-token rank collapse to vanishing query/key gradients under uniform attention, and show that depth-dependent residual scaling preserves correlations under their forward-analysis assumptions, including linear activations. They provide preliminary evidence that gradient-magnitude imbalance contributes to Adam's advantage and that residual scaling plus inverse-temperature adjustment improves SGD translation performance; they do not establish equal training speed or a complete explanation of Adam's advantage.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies Transformer signal propagation and translation optimization, not the original CIFAR classification or feedforward-network recipes. It uses a uniform-attention assumption for theoretical results, linear activations for forward-propagation theory, Transformer residual scaling, and an IWSLT14 translation task.
record.method_sensitivity: Residual scaling and depth; PRE-LN versus POST-LN versus no layer normalization; input variance and token correlation; inverse temperature; number of Transformer blocks; optimizer.

fits_no_version.finding: Transformer token alignment increases with depth, while depth-dependent residual scaling preserves correlations and improves query/key gradient propagation. Figure 1 additionally reports translation training-loss trajectories.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Depth-dependent residual scaling can prevent token alignment and associated optimization difficulties in Transformers.

fits_no_version.finding: Residual scaling and inverse-temperature adjustment improve SGD translation BLEU; the combined recipe reaches 35.69 versus 31.36 for SGD POST-LN and 35.39 for Adam POST-LN, with different training budgets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectural scaling can improve SGD Transformer translation performance and enable training deeper Transformers without layer normalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Uniform-attention predictions approximate representation norms and parameter-gradient norms, with closer agreement at smaller input variance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Uniform-attention approximations describe Transformer initialization signal propagation under restricted input and initialization conditions.

record.problems: The principal gradient and forward-propagation claims depend on a uniform-attention assumption; the forward analysis also assumes linear activations. The text notes that extending correlation formulas to ReLU feedforward layers is technically difficult. Empirical curves are mostly figure-only, and translation BLEU is averaged over 5 runs without reported error bars.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying results omitted. Cited prior-work outcomes were excluded.

untested.parts: All parts: CIFAR training classification error, random or corrupted labels, model size and training-recipe qualifications.
All parts: two-layer ReLU teacher-student local minima and additional student neurons.
All parts: plain versus residual convolutional training-error degradation, extended training, very deep plain tanh networks and Fixup residual networks.
All parts: activation-matched initialization effects on plain-network learning speed and trainable depth, orthogonal versus Gaussian tanh initialization and 10,000-layer plain convolutional training.
All parts: initial stability limits, loss recovery, curvature reduction, edge-of-stability dynamics and divergence.
All parts: batch-normalization accuracy-speed and learning-rate comparisons, and Fixup residual-network speed and stability without normalization.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for these versions. Its related Transformer findings do not warrant scope limits on claims explicitly about different architectures and outcomes. No qualifying version result requires a missing-row entry.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 training classification error; corrupted or random labels; model size, early stopping, and regularization effects.
Teacher-student ReLU local minima and student width relative to teacher width.

Does not compare plain convolutional networks against residual networks on ImageNet or CIFAR-10, or measure training classification error. Its Transformer experiments concern token correlation and gradient propagation; its translation experiment compares optimizer and architecture recipes.

Does not test activation-matched initializations in plain feedforward networks, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, or 10,000-layer convolutional networks. It studies Transformer initialization and residual scaling.
Learning rates above the stability limit, catapult dynamics, sharpness hovering at a threshold, and divergence.

No controlled comparison measuring batch normalization's accuracy-speed benefit or learning-rate tolerance; it discusses layer normalization in Transformers and compares translation recipes without isolating normalization's effect.

rows.subject: POST-LN Transformer
rows.stage_stated: trained on IWSLT’14 De-En translation task
rows.operation_detail: Measured cosine of the angle between tokens during training without adequate residual scaling.
rows.measure: Cosine angle between token representations over training steps
rows.value: Figure shows token alignment increasing with depth; exact values figure only.
rows.note: The text says increasing depth raises alignment at initialization and can inhibit training; the plot shows the cosine trajectories, without tabulated values.
rows.check: Token alignment in residual Transformers does not measure V3's plain-versus-residual convolutional training error or V4's plain-network initialization effect. Figure 1 also includes scaled runs and training-loss curves, omitted from this row.

rows.subject: Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Compared token cosine and relative query/key and value gradient norms across depth with and without residual scaling.
rows.measure: Token cosine angle and relative gradient norms for queries/keys and values
rows.baseline: Corresponding first-layer gradient norms for relative-gradient plots; token-cosine baseline not stated.
rows.value: Without scaling, token cosine rises toward alignment and query/key gradients diminish with depth; scaling stabilizes token correlations and gradient propagation. Exact values figure only.
rows.note: Figure caption states query/key gradients diminish with depth and values show the opposite; the residual scaling comparison is shown graphically.
rows.check: Initialization correlations and relative gradient norms in POST-LN Transformers cannot establish the training outcomes specified by V3 or V4.

rows.subject: Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Measured token correlation with and without residual scaling for no layer normalization, PRE-LN, and POST-LN.
rows.value: Figure shows correlation increasing with depth without scaling; with scaling correlation remains lower. PRE-LN without scaling has a slower increase than POST-LN or No-LN. Exact values figure only.
rows.note: The authors state PRE-LN seems to alleviate the rate of increase without residual scaling; layer normalization does not significantly affect correlation evolution when scaling is used.
rows.check: Transformer token correlation is a different measure from training error or training speed. PRE-LN and POST-LN are layer normalization, whereas V6 concerns batch normalization and Fixup residual-network training.

rows.subject: Transformer encoder-decoder
rows.operation_detail: Trained with SGD and residual scaling, without layer normalization, and evaluated BLEU on IWSLT14 German-to-English.
rows.uncertainty: Average BLEU across 5 runs; no error bar stated.
rows.note: Translation BLEU is a task metric rather than training classification error; the comparison shows a no-normalization, residual-scaled SGD recipe can train this Transformer.
rows.check: BLEU for a residual-scaled Transformer recipe does not measure the specified plain-network initialization or convolutional depth-degradation effects. Residual scales are trainable. SGD also receives 250K updates versus Adam's 100K, so the table cannot establish equal training speed.

rows.subject: Transformer encoder-decoder
rows.operation_detail: Trained with SGD and inverse temperature scaling in addition to residual scaling; evaluated BLEU.
rows.uncertainty: Average BLEU across 5 runs; no error bar stated.
rows.note: This recipe includes inverse temperature scaling as well as residual scaling, so the result does not isolate initialization alone.
rows.check: The proposed recipe combines residual scaling, removal of layer normalization and inverse-temperature adjustment. Its BLEU measures recipe performance, not any specified version's effect.

rows.subject: Transformer encoder-decoder
rows.operation_detail: Trained with Adam and POST-LN; evaluated BLEU.
rows.uncertainty: Average BLEU across 5 runs; no error bar stated.
rows.note: Comparator score; the table does not supply a no-normalization or alternate-initialization baseline for this method.
rows.check: This is an experimental recipe comparator; its BLEU alone provides no qualifying initialization, training-error or training-speed comparison.

rows.subject: Transformer encoder-decoder
rows.operation_detail: Trained with Adam and PRE-LN; evaluated BLEU.
rows.uncertainty: Average BLEU across 5 runs; no error bar stated.
rows.note: Comparator score; the table does not isolate the effect of normalization.
rows.check: This is an experimental recipe comparator using layer normalization; its BLEU does not test V3, V4 or batch normalization.

rows.subject: Transformer encoder-decoder
rows.operation_detail: Trained using ReZero initialization; evaluated BLEU.
rows.uncertainty: Average BLEU across 5 runs; no error bar stated.
rows.check: ReZero Transformer BLEU is a recipe comparator, not a measurement of any specified version. Figure 6 identifies Adam as its optimizer.

rows.subject: Transformer encoder-decoder
rows.uncertainty: Average BLEU across 5 runs; no error bar stated.
rows.check: T-Fixup Transformer BLEU is a recipe comparator; it does not test the Fixup residual-network speed and stability clause. Figure 6 identifies Adam as its optimizer.

rows.subject: Transformer encoder-decoder
rows.size_stated: Varying number of Transformer blocks; Figure 6 gives no exact depths per point in text
rows.operation_detail: Compared BLEU as the number of Transformer blocks increased across training methods.

conditions.value: SGD POST-LN, SGD res-scale, SGD temperature, Adam PRE-LN, Adam POST-LN, T-Fixup, ReZero

rows.measure: BLEU score by number of Transformer blocks
rows.value: Figure only; text says proposed method can train deeper networks without layer normalization.
rows.note: The figure compares depth scaling for methods; precise curve values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Depth-dependent BLEU across residual Transformer recipes does not test plain convolutional training-error degradation or activation-matched initialization in plain networks. Figure 6 spans 6–20 blocks; each count includes encoder self-attention, decoder self-attention and decoder cross-attention layers.

rows.subject: Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Compared activation-norm distributions under uniform attention and two settings without the uniform-attention assumption.

conditions.value: i.i.d. Gaussian entries simulating an embedding layer

rows.measure: Distribution and empirical mean of final representation Frobenius norm
rows.value: Figure only; text says uniform-attention approximation is excellent when input standard deviation is 1/√d, and deviations occur when it is increased.
rows.uncertainty: 1000 weight samples; no error bars stated.
rows.note: This checks an approximation for signal propagation, not classification training error.
rows.check: This validates a uniform-attention approximation rather than a claim version. Figure 10 measures squared Frobenius norm, not unsquared Frobenius norm.

rows.subject: Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Compared automatic-differentiation gradient norms with theoretical predictions while varying architecture and input properties.

conditions.value: hidden dimension, sequence length, input correlation, input variance

rows.measure: Query/key gradient norms against theoretical predictions
rows.baseline: Theoretical results based on uniform-attention assumption
rows.value: Figure only; text says predictions agree well with true gradients, with tighter agreement for smaller input standard deviation.
rows.note: The authors identify greater input variance as a source of deviation from the uniform-attention approximation.
rows.check: Agreement between theoretical and automatic-differentiation gradients validates an approximation; it does not measure faster learning or greater trainable depth.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Transformer signal-propagation analysis and IWSLT14 translation experiments
reader_labels.reason: The paper finds that residual connections alone do not prevent high token alignment at large depth, while depth-dependent scaling preserves correlations; it also reports successful training recipes for deeper Transformers without normalization. Rows R1–R5 and R10.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Transformer initialization analysis with depth-dependent residual scaling
reader_labels.reason: The analysis and figures report that residual scaling preserves token correlations and stabilizes gradient propagation as depth grows; translation results show scaled recipes can train without normalization. Rows R2–R5, R10.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Transformer token-correlation analysis under layer-normalization variants
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports PRE-LN slows correlation growth without residual scaling, while normalization does not significantly affect correlation evolution when residual scaling is used; these are correlation results, not the version's accuracy-speed or learning-rate-tolerance measure. Row R3.
